1:
Whether land is really being divided is the first question. Gill denies it: this fits neither the division at the conquest, nor the return from Babylon, nor anything expected at the latter-day conversion, nor the reading that makes it a type of the heavenly inheritance; since the whole vision concerns the church on earth, the allotment must be the settling of Christ's kingdom through the world. Henry agrees that it was never accomplished in the Jewish state, and finds it fulfilled in the Christian church, as new as this division is unlike the old one and enlarged by the coming in of the Gentiles. Clarke keeps it on the ground, each family resettling by its former allotment, and observes that the land was not divided afresh by lot after the captivity; what is described is only the provision for temple, priests and prince. Ellicott notes that dividing by lot implies nothing of chance, each tribe being later assigned its portion by name.

The unit of measurement is left unstated in the original and the readers do not agree. Ellicott argues for reeds, from the size given elsewhere for the temple precincts and from the mention of cubits in the next verse, which implies a different measure everywhere else; the twenty-five thousand is then a hundred and fifty thousand cubits, over forty-seven statute miles. Wesley reckons in cubits throughout and gets twelve miles and a half. The breadth is disputed too: the Greek reads twenty thousand where the Hebrew has ten, and Keil and Delitzsch print the figure with a query beside it, while Ellicott declines the change, the whole width being twenty-five thousand made of ten for the Levites, ten for the priests and five for the city.

The size of the priests' share strikes Ellicott as remarkable. More than forty-seven miles by nearly nineteen, it is enormously larger than the thirteen cities the older law gave them. He reports the suggestion that it replaces the tithes, which this prophet never mentions, and rejects it, the law of tithes being ancient and so large a change unlikely to pass without a word. His own account is that the priests' land is enlarged in proportion to the sanctuary, both meant to set out the precedence of worship.

One clause defeats him and he mends it. The Levites' portion ends with words that admit of no satisfactory explanation, Transposing two letters in one word and altering a letter in the next yields a possession of gates to dwell in, gates being an ordinary word for cities. Gill takes the verse simply, as a second portion of the same measure.

The city and the prince close the section. Ellicott observes that the city's ground is called a profane place though it belongs to the oblation, and then makes a striking negative point: nothing identifies this city with Jerusalem, its position is different, and Jerusalem seems to have faded from the prophet's sight, like the ark, in this vision of the church to come. Wesley assumes the opposite, taking it for the capital and its citizens. Gill reads it as the civil state of God's people under the spiritual reign. On the prince the split reappears: Gill will have nothing but the Messiah, while Clarke says the word means the chief magistrate, the Jews having had neither king nor prince after the captivity. Ellicott explains the plural in the promise against oppression as conceiving the royal office as a succession, though one king is to reign for ever, and traces the old oppression to kings who had no domain and so took property by violence. Clarke names the same abuse in his own terms, exorbitant taxes for profligate courts and subsidies paid out of the temple. Henry draws a lesson from the measuring: the borders were fixed so the sanctuary should not in time engross the whole land.
9:
The charge to the princes is read as plain civil justice. Henry treats the verses as rules of distributive and commutative justice, on the ground that godliness without honesty is only a form of godliness; the princes have enriched themselves by spoil and fleeced the flock instead of feeding it, and the point of let it suffice you is that no prescription justifies a wrong. He turns the excuse round: instead of pleading that they have long been accustomed to oppress and may therefore continue, let them say they have long been accustomed to it and let the time past suffice, dropping wrongful demands, turning out the men who do violence, and easing the heaviest taxes. Clarke widens the address to every ruler on earth: take away your exactions and abolish oppressive taxes, the people being God's. Gill keeps the promise as well as the rebuke, expecting Christian princes with ample salaries to support their dignity, content with them and not encroaching.

The weights and measures are a matter of arithmetic and of honesty at once. Gill makes their enforcement the civil magistrate's business. Clarke reads the passage as a warning not to bring home the standards they had grown used to in captivity, but to return to those prescribed to their forefathers. Ellicott gives the terms their history: the ephah appears early and looks Egyptian, and served for dry measure, while the bath is not met with until much later and was the largest liquid measure; that the two are of one capacity, each a tenth of the homer, matters for comparing the Hebrew scales, though their absolute value is exceedingly hard to fix. His figures show how hard: by one ancient historian the homer comes to eighty-six thousand gallons and by the rabbis to forty-two thousand, and modern estimates differ nearly as widely. The homer, ten ephahs, must also be carefully distinguished from the omer, a tenth of one, the words being quite different in Hebrew.

The figures for the maneh divide them sharply. Henry, following a computation he cites with confidence, makes the shekel twenty gerahs and half a Roman ounce, and explains that the maneh weighed a hundred shekels as a weight, shown by comparing two accounts of the same gold shields, but only sixty as money; hence the twenty, twenty-five and fifteen of this verse, three coins of those weights making one pound. Ellicott finds the clause extremely obscure. The first half only restates the old law about the gerahs, but the maneh occurs in very few places, its value is unknown, and if the text stands the most he will say is that three different manehs may have been in use, adding at once that there is no other evidence.

What the people pay and what the prince does with it are new. Ellicott points out that the contribution is a regular tax to the prince so he can furnish the sanctuary offerings, called a heave offering like the land and fixed at a sixtieth of the grain, a hundredth of the oil and a two-hundredth of the flock, all out of the year's increase; and that the prince's obligation to provide the festal sacrifices is entirely new, since the older law said nothing about where they were to come from, so what had been freewill offering becomes established duty. Gill draws the opposite conclusion from the same fractions: they show the Mosaic dispensation abrogated, tithes of all things being no longer required but only a sixtieth, a hundredth and one lamb in two hundred, which he takes for the moderate maintenance of Gospel ministers, no one being exempt from contributing. On the prince himself he parts from the others, refusing both the high priest and the civil ruler for the Messiah, Prince and Priest together, whose one sacrifice answers all the many that typified it.
18:
This calendar is not the old one. Clarke says flatly that there is nothing of this cleansing of the sanctuary in the law of Moses and that it seems a new ceremony, perhaps an annual one; Gill says the same of the seventh-day rule, citing a rabbi who owns as much. Ellicott generalises and draws a conclusion. The rest of the chapter and the opening of the next set out the ritual for particular occasions, and in every case the departures from the older law are remarkable, as is the silence about the Feast of Weeks and the Day of Atonement. A priest could not have been ignorant of the law here, so the changes must be deliberate; and like the changes in the division of the land they seem meant to show the vision ideal. No attempt, he adds, was ever made to carry them out.

The changes he sets out item by item. The older law required a he-goat as sin offering for the first of every month, and two on the Day of Atonement; of all this only the offering for the beginning of the first month survives, with a second for the seventh day that the law knows nothing of, and both are bullocks rather than goats. The ritual of the blood is altered to match. The law gave no special direction for the monthly sin offerings, since they fell under the ordinary rule of sprinkling on the sides of the altar; only when the victim was a bullock was the blood brought inside and sprinkled seven times before the veil. Here it goes instead on the posts of the house, the corners of the settle of the altar and the posts of the inner gate.

What the seventh day's offering is for Ellicott treats as a real question. The first day's is expressly to cleanse the sanctuary, but this one is for everyone who errs and for the simple, those who sinned thoughtlessly rather than wilfully, and yet the verse ends by saying they shall reconcile the house, more literally make atonement for it. He answers by looking to the Day of Atonement, which these two days seem meant to replace: those sacrifices were for the sins of priests and people and for the tabernacle at once, the one involving the other, since the holy place needed purifying because of the sins of the people among whom it stood. Clarke glosses the simple as one wanting understanding to conduct himself properly. Gill reads the blood as an emblem of the blood of Christ.

The two feasts that remain are altered in opposite directions. On the passover Ellicott finds the appointment quite in accord with the old institution, though a peculiarity of the original has led some to infer, unnecessarily, that it was to run seven weeks; Keil and Delitzsch take the wording to mean the feast is kept as first appointed, with the meal in the evening. But the sacrifices differ throughout. Nothing is said of the paschal lamb, which may have gone without saying; the daily he-goat becomes a bullock on the first day and a goat afterwards; two bullocks, a ram and seven lambs become seven bullocks and seven rams; and where the law asked graded portions of meal, a whole ephah now goes to every victim, fourteen a day with as many measures of oil, so the passover offerings come out much richer than the law required. The seventh-month feast goes the other way. Ellicott identifies it with the feast of booths, unnamed, he supposes, because living in booths is to cease, and finds the ritual simplified, the eighth day dropped and the sacrifices much reduced. Clarke sees only that the prince does here exactly what he did at the other.
